relationship: watchman image and its prophetic application
rationale: The land's people appoint a watchman in the source's illustration. In the earlier commission God appoints Ezekiel as Israel's watchman to hear and convey His word; the appointing authority differs.

relationship: parallel trumpet warning of approaching judgment
rationale: The watchman sounds a trumpet when the sword approaches. Jeremiah's appointed watchers also call for hearing the trumpet, and the people's refusal is followed by threatened evils.

relationship: parallel accountability for refusing a trumpet warning
rationale: The hearer who neglects the trumpet is overtaken by the sword and bears responsibility for his blood. Jeremiah likewise connects refusal to hear the watchers and God's words with ensuing judgment.

relationship: related preservation of life through heeding warning
rationale: The source contrasts the negligent hearer's responsibility with one who takes care and rescues his life. The earlier commission likewise says a warned righteous person who does not sin will live.

relationship: watchman's blood responsibility applied to prophetic warning
rationale: A watchman who fails to signal must answer for the victim's blood even though the victim dies in his own lawlessness. The earlier commission assigns Ezekiel the same responsibility when he withholds the warning.

relationship: contrast between withheld warning and discharge of responsibility
rationale: The negligent watchman must answer for another's blood. Paul declares himself clean from everyone's blood because he did not hold back God's whole purpose, presenting the corresponding positive claim about faithfully delivering a message.

relationship: repeated appointment as Israel's watchman
rationale: Both passages appoint Ezekiel as watchman for Israel's house and require him to hear God's word. The earlier passage explicitly adds conveying God's warning.

relationship: repeated warning and blood accountability
rationale: Both passages announce death to the lawless person and require his blood from the prophet's hand if the prophet fails to warn him to turn from his way.

relationship: repeated distinction between rejected warning and the prophet's responsibility
rationale: Both passages say that a warned person who refuses to turn dies in his own wrongdoing, while the prophet who delivered the warning rescues his own life.

relationship: covenant warning and confession of wasting away in sin
rationale: Israel says its lawless deeds lie upon it and asks how it can live while wasting away. Leviticus predicts that survivors waste away because of their sins and then confess their own and their fathers' sins.

relationship: repeated preference for repentance and life
rationale: Both passages deny that God desires the lawless person's death and instead call for turning from the evil way and living. The source directly addresses Israel with an urgent call to turn.

relationship: parallel reversal of standing through present conduct
rationale: Both passages contrast turning from lawlessness with turning away from righteousness. The source says former lawlessness will not harm the person who turns, while Ezekiel 18 explicitly promises life; former righteousness does not protect the person who now acts lawlessly.

relationship: repeated warning that former righteous deeds do not excuse new wrongdoing
rationale: The source describes a person trusting in prior righteousness while acting lawlessly. Both passages say that the former righteous acts will not be remembered and that the person dies in the new wrongdoing.

relationship: parallel turning from lawlessness toward righteous conduct
rationale: Both passages describe a lawless person turning from wrongdoing and practicing righteousness. The source's sentence continues into the following unit's concrete acts and assurance of life.

relationship: particular legal counterpart for returning a pledge
rationale: The source includes returning a pledge among the acts that accompany a changed life. Deuteronomy specifically requires returning a poor debtor's garment at sunset and calls that act mercy before God.

relationship: repeated non-remembrance of former sins after repentance
rationale: Both passages say that the former transgressions of the person who now practices righteousness will not be remembered, and connect that righteous conduct with life.

relationship: repeated dispute over whose way is crooked
rationale: Israel's complaint that the Lord's way is not straight is answered by identifying the people's own way as the crooked one. The earlier oracle presents the same accusation and response.

relationship: repeated consequence of turning from righteousness
rationale: Both passages say that a righteous person who turns from righteousness to transgression dies in the wrongdoing he committed.

relationship: repeated preservation of life through turning from lawlessness
rationale: Both passages describe the lawless person turning to judgment and righteousness and living. The earlier passage explicitly states that this person has preserved his life.

relationship: repeated complaint followed by individual judgment
rationale: Both passages repeat Israel's objection to God's way and announce judgment on each person according to that person's way. The earlier passage additionally calls for turning from impiety.

relationship: narrative arrival corresponding to the promised survivor's report
rationale: The source records a survivor from Jerusalem announcing that the city has been captured. The earlier oracle anticipates a survivor coming to announce the loss and the prophet's mouth opening toward him.

relationship: narrative counterpart to the promised opening of the prophet's mouth
rationale: The earlier oracle promises that Ezekiel will speak to the survivor and no longer be mute. The source records the opening of his mouth around the survivor's arrival and the ending of its restraint.

relationship: different appeals to the single ancestor Abraham
rationale: The inhabitants argue from Abraham being one while they are many to claim the land. Isaiah also recalls Abraham as one whom God called and multiplied, but locates the increase in God's blessing.

relationship: contrast to security claimed through Abraham
rationale: The inhabitants appeal to Abraham and their greater numbers as grounds for possession. John's warning refuses ancestry in Abraham as a substitute for repentance; Ezekiel's surrounding oracle likewise announces judgment for their abominations.

relationship: particular covenant judgments of beasts, sword and death
rationale: The source assigns sword, wild beasts and death to people in different locations. Leviticus likewise threatens consuming beasts, a covenant-avenging sword and death within cities; its sequence and locations differ.

relationship: covenant desolation reflected in the land's announced ruin
rationale: Both passages announce desolate land. Ezekiel particularly describes empty mountains and the collapse of arrogant strength, while Leviticus includes scattering among nations.

relationship: related judgment connecting polluted worship with a desolate land
rationale: The source attributes the land's devastation to the people's abominations. Leviticus places ruined images, desolate holy places, cities and land within the consequences of covenant disobedience.

relationship: explicit contrast between hearing the word and doing it
rationale: The assembled people hear Ezekiel's words but do not do them. James warns against being hearers only and distinguishes the forgetful hearer from the person who acts.

relationship: parallel warning about hearing without obedience
rationale: Ezekiel's listeners hear his words without doing them. Jesus likens hearing His words without practicing them to a house founded on sand that falls under the storm.

relationship: related exposure of hearing without action
rationale: Ezekiel's listeners enjoy his words like a finely tuned instrument but do not act. James contrasts mere hearing with doing; he does not supply Ezekiel's musical comparison.

relationship: recognition of prophetic speech through its outcome
rationale: The coming event will make the people recognize that a prophet was among them. Deuteronomy likewise tests a purported divine word by whether it happens, describing the negative case of an unfulfilled prediction.

relationship: shared criticism of shepherds feeding themselves
rationale: The source contrasts shepherds feeding themselves with their duty to feed the sheep. Jude also describes the criticized people as shepherding themselves at communal feasts, in a different setting.

relationship: parallel exploitation of sheep by those responsible for them
rationale: Ezekiel's shepherds consume milk, wear wool and slaughter animals without feeding the flock. Zechariah describes sheep destined for slaughter, profitable sellers and unfeeling shepherds; the specific benefits differ.

relationship: close parallel lists of failed shepherding duties
rationale: Both passages fault a shepherd for failing to seek the scattered or lost and heal or bind the injured. Ezekiel also says the strong were worn down with toil, while Zechariah describes devouring flesh and wrenching ankle bones.

relationship: parallel scattering and exposure of an uncared-for flock
rationale: The source's sheep scatter for lack of shepherds and become food for beasts. In John the hired worker abandons the sheep and the wolf seizes and scatters them, because the worker does not care.

relationship: parallel scattered flock neglected by its shepherds
rationale: Both oracles describe God's scattered sheep. Ezekiel says no one seeks or turns them back, while Jeremiah faults shepherds who did not visit them and announces God's gathering of the remnant.

relationship: parallel indictment of shepherds for the flock's loss
rationale: Ezekiel charges the shepherds with feeding themselves while the sheep become plunder and prey. Jeremiah likewise holds shepherds accountable for scattering and destroying the flock without visiting it.

relationship: parallel divine accountability of shepherds and recovery of the flock
rationale: God requires the sheep from negligent shepherds and rescues them in Ezekiel. Jeremiah similarly announces judgment on the shepherds and God's own receiving and establishing of the remnant.

relationship: related image of seeking and recovering a lost sheep
rationale: God promises personally to seek His sheep. Jesus' parable describes a shepherd going after a lost sheep until he finds it and then rejoicing; the source concerns the scattered people as a flock.

relationship: related shepherd's search through the flock's separation
rationale: Ezekiel compares God's search for scattered people with a shepherd seeking separated sheep amid gloom. The parable likewise depicts a shepherd actively going after the lost sheep, without Ezekiel's cloud-and-gloom setting.

relationship: parallel gathering from countries and restoration to pasture and land
rationale: Both passages gather Israel from the lands of dispersion and restore the people to their own land and pasture. Jeremiah additionally promises new shepherds and a righteous Davidic ruler.

relationship: shared divine shepherding into nourishing pasture and rest
rationale: The source promises good pasture and a place where the sheep rest on Israel's mountain. The psalm describes the Lord shepherding the speaker into green growth and beside water of rest.

relationship: shared personal care and rest under the divine shepherd
rationale: God Himself promises to feed His sheep and give them rest. The psalm likewise names the Lord as the shepherd who nourishes the speaker and provides a resting place.

relationship: contrast between promised care and failed shepherding
rationale: God promises to seek, restore, bind and strengthen the flock, guarding the strong. Zechariah's shepherd fails to attend, seek, heal or guide and instead consumes the flock. Ezekiel's guarding of the strong is preserved.

relationship: related recovery of the lost sheep
rationale: The source's first promise is to seek the lost and bring back the wandering. The parable depicts a shepherd finding a lost sheep and relates the rejoicing to a sinner's repentance; its scope is narrower than Ezekiel's whole list of care.

relationship: related divine distinction within a flock representing people
rationale: Ezekiel distinguishes among sheep, rams and male goats. Matthew depicts the gathered nations being separated as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; the target develops a judgment scene with right and left positions not stated in Ezekiel.

relationship: same-chapter accusation recast as its consequence for the flock
rationale: The source accuses the well-fed sheep of trampling pasture and muddying water. The next unit repeats those acts from the dependent sheep's perspective: they ate the trampled pasture and drank the disturbed water.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between privileged consumption and the flock's remainder
rationale: The source describes the sheep eating trampled pasture and drinking disturbed water. The preceding accusation identifies the privileged animals that enjoyed the good pasture and settled water before spoiling what remained.

relationship: related judgment portrayed through distinguishing among flock members
rationale: Ezekiel distinguishes strong sheep from weak sheep amid the indictment of abusive flock members. Matthew also represents judgment of people through a shepherd separating a flock, but distinguishes sheep from goats rather than strong from weak sheep.

relationship: same-chapter extension of blame from shepherds to abusive flock members
rationale: The source accuses animals of using shoulders and horns to force out failing sheep. Earlier the shepherds were faulted for not strengthening the weak and wearing down the strong; both expose failures to care for vulnerable members, with different actors.

relationship: parallel restoration of a flock to safety
rationale: Ezekiel promises to save the sheep from plunder and judge within the flock. Jeremiah promises restored pasture and shepherds under whom the sheep will no longer fear. Jeremiah does not include the source's judgment between rams.

relationship: repeated promise of David and one shepherd
rationale: Both passages designate God's servant David as ruler or shepherd and place the people under one shepherd. The later passage also connects this leadership with keeping God's ordinances.

relationship: related promise of unity under one shepherd
rationale: Ezekiel promises one shepherd, called God's servant David. Jesus says the sheep He brings will become one flock with one shepherd. This links the shared shepherd-and-unity language without treating the passages as identical wording.

relationship: repeated combination of Davidic rule and covenant belonging
rationale: Both passages place David among the people as ruler and declare that the Lord is their God. The later oracle expands this with an everlasting covenant and God's dwelling among them.

relationship: shared promise of peace and removal of harmful beasts
rationale: Ezekiel promises a covenant of peace with David and removal of harmful beasts so people may rest safely. Leviticus likewise promises peace, safe lying down and removal of harmful animals, without naming David.

relationship: shared promise of beneficial rain
rationale: Ezekiel promises rain of blessing around God's mountain. Leviticus promises rain in its season and resulting produce; the source does not itself specify that seasonal wording.

relationship: related fruitfulness and peaceful settlement
rationale: Both passages promise fruitful trees and productive land. Ezekiel joins this with dwelling in hope of peace, while Leviticus promises secure dwelling. Ezekiel also announces deliverance from enslavers, which is not contained in this selected target.

relationship: close parallel breaking the enslaving yoke
rationale: Ezekiel promises to shatter the people's yoke and rescue them from enslavers. Leviticus recalls God's release of Israel from Egyptian slavery and the shattering of their yoke.

relationship: close parallel security from beasts and terror
rationale: Both passages promise that harmful beasts will no longer threaten the people and that they will dwell or lie down without anyone frightening them.

relationship: parallel relief from famine and national reproach
rationale: Ezekiel promises a plant of peace, no longer perishing by famine and relief from the nations' reproach. Joel promises grain, wine and oil, abundant eating and an end to reproach; it does not identify Ezekiel's plant.

relationship: shared covenant declaration of God and His people
rationale: Both passages join God's being their God with their being His people. Ezekiel explicitly identifies this people as Israel's house.

relationship: close identification of God's people as His sheep
rationale: Ezekiel calls the addressed people God's sheep and flock. The psalm similarly identifies the people God made as His people and the sheep of His pasture.

relationship: geographical and ancestral counterpart for Mount Seir
rationale: The oracle is directed against Mount Seir. Genesis locates Esau, identified as Edom, in that mountain; Ezekiel 35:15 itself also pairs Mount Seir with Idumea.

relationship: parallel desolation of Esau's territory and Idumea
rationale: Ezekiel announces that Mount Seir will become a wilderness. Malachi likewise assigns Esau's territories to desolation and threatens to overthrow Idumea's rebuilding; Genesis 36:8-9 supplies the Seir-Esau connection.

relationship: parallel desolation of settlements in Idumea
rationale: Ezekiel announces desolate cities and wilderness. Malachi reports Idumea's plan to rebuild deserted places and God's declaration that He will overthrow what they build.

relationship: parallel condemnation of hostility during Israel's disaster
rationale: Ezekiel charges Seir with lasting enmity and treacherous attack during Israel's final time of injustice. Obadiah records violence against Jacob and participation in Jerusalem's calamity, then forbids destroying those escaping and shutting in fugitives.

relationship: related requital for shedding blood
rationale: The source announces that blood will pursue the people who sinned unto blood. Genesis requires an accounting for human blood and describes the shedding of the blood-shedder's own blood in return.

relationship: close parallel judgment on Mount Seir and Idumea
rationale: God announces Mount Seir's desolation and the destruction of human beings and livestock. The earlier Idumea oracle likewise announces destruction of human and animal and the land becoming wilderness; Ezekiel 35:15 explicitly joins Mount Seir and all Idumea. The target additionally mentions Thaiman and the sword.

relationship: related judgment filling Idumea's terrain with the wounded
rationale: Ezekiel fills hills, ravines and plains with the sword-wounded. Isaiah describes wounded and dead, blood-soaked mountains and a sword descending upon Idumea; the locations and imagery are not identical.

relationship: parallel enduring desolation of Idumea
rationale: Ezekiel calls Seir an everlasting wilderness with uninhabited cities. Isaiah likewise describes Idumea's land burning and deserted for generations, with vegetation and wild creatures replacing settled cities.

relationship: adjacent-oracle parallel claim to possess God's land
rationale: Seir claims two nations and countries as its inheritance even though the Lord is there. The following oracle again condemns enemies, explicitly including Idumea, for assigning God's land to themselves; it does not name the source's two nations separately.

relationship: parallel repayment according to the aggressor's own conduct
rationale: Ezekiel announces judgment according to Seir's hostility. Obadiah likewise says that what the aggressor did will be repaid upon the aggressor's own head.

relationship: adjacent-oracle repetition of predatory claims over Israel's land
rationale: The source quotes the boast that Israel's desolate mountains were given for the enemy's food. The following oracle repeats the enemy's possession claim and condemns Idumea's rejoicing and plunder.

relationship: related divine response to an enemy's arrogant speech
rationale: Ezekiel says the Lord heard Seir's grand speech against Him. The Kings oracle likewise identifies Assyria's raised voice against Israel's Holy One and says its arrogance reached God's ears; the enemies and occasions differ.

relationship: parallel announced consumption of Idumea's associated house
rationale: Ezekiel announces that Mount Seir and all Idumea will be consumed. Obadiah, addressed to Idumea, depicts Esau's house as stubble consumed by Jacob's fire and Joseph's flame. Its particular wording about no bearer of fire is preserved.

relationship: repeated address to Israel's mountains in contrasting oracles
rationale: Both directives direct Ezekiel to prophesy to Israel's mountains and call them to hear God's word. The earlier address announces a sword, whereas the present address introduces the restoration of the same land.

relationship: adjacent-oracle repetition of the enemy's possession claim
rationale: The enemy celebrates gaining the desolate land as a possession. The preceding Seir oracle quotes the same kind of claim over the countries and Israel's devastated mountains; its two nations are not separately named here.

relationship: parallel national humiliation after hostile occupation
rationale: Ezekiel describes Israel's land becoming the nations' possession and a reproach on people's tongues. The psalm likewise joins invasion of God's inheritance and Jerusalem's devastation with neighbors' sneering and ridicule.

relationship: repeated geographical address with reversal of the land's condition
rationale: Both oracles address Israel's mountains, hills and ravines and speak of devastated settlements. The earlier oracle announces their ruin; the present oracle addresses the ruined places before promising their recovery.

relationship: parallel judgment on Idumea's conduct toward Judah's calamity
rationale: Ezekiel condemns Idumea for claiming God's land with rejoicing and destructive plunder. Obadiah describes Idumea's involvement in Jerusalem's calamity, forbids rejoicing and joining the attacks, and announces repayment according to its conduct.

relationship: related reproach of Israel and appeal to divine jealousy
rationale: Ezekiel's Lord speaks in jealousy and wrath because the land bore the nations' reproaches. The psalm places the neighbors' ridicule beside its question about God's anger and jealousy; it is a plea, whereas Ezekiel announces God's response.

relationship: parallel requital of the neighbors' insult
rationale: Ezekiel says the surrounding nations will receive their own dishonor. The psalm asks God to repay neighboring peoples for the insult they directed against Him; its sevenfold measure is not stated in Ezekiel.

relationship: parallel restored Israel consuming its land's fruit
rationale: Ezekiel promises that the approaching people will consume the mountains' grapes and fruit. Amos likewise joins the reversal of Israel's captivity with planting vineyards and gardens and enjoying their wine and fruit.

relationship: parallel renewal of cultivation in restored land
rationale: Ezekiel promises that God's favorable attention will result in the land being cultivated and sown. Amos describes restored Israelites planting vineyards and gardens as they rebuild and inhabit the ruined land.

relationship: parallel rebuilding of devastated settlements
rationale: Ezekiel promises inhabited cities and rebuilding of devastated land. Isaiah likewise promises renewal of deserted cities and places desolated for generations; it does not specify Ezekiel's multiplication of all Israel's house.

relationship: parallel restoration of human and animal populations
rationale: Ezekiel promises to multiply humans and livestock and restore former settlement. Jeremiah similarly promises to sow Israel and Judah with human and livestock seed, followed by God's watching to build and plant.

relationship: parallel secure possession of restored land
rationale: Ezekiel promises Israel possession of the land and says the land will no longer be bereaved of the people. Amos promises to plant the people on their given land without their being uprooted again; the images express security differently.

relationship: repeated description of the land as devouring inhabitants
rationale: Ezekiel quotes the accusation that the land devours human beings. The scouts' dismaying report in Numbers uses the same description of a land that devours its inhabitants; the speakers and occasions differ.

relationship: reversal of the land-devouring accusation
rationale: Ezekiel promises that the land will no longer eat human beings or bereave its nation. Numbers preserves the scouts' earlier accusation that the land devours its inhabitants; Ezekiel's promise negates that characterization.

relationship: parallel removal of the nations' reproach
rationale: Ezekiel promises that the land will no longer bear the peoples' reproaches. Joel likewise promises that God will no longer give His people over as a reproach among the nations, alongside renewed food supplies.

relationship: ritual-uncleanness imagery applied to Israel's conduct
rationale: Ezekiel compares Israel's defiling conduct and idols with the uncleanness of a woman sitting apart. Leviticus supplies concrete regulations for menstrual uncleanness of that kind; it does not itself equate menstruation with Israel's wrongdoing.

relationship: parallel covenant judgment of international scattering
rationale: Ezekiel describes God scattering Israel among nations as judgment for its conduct. Leviticus threatens scattering among the nations together with ruined land and cities as a consequence of covenant disobedience.

relationship: parallel dishonor of God's name among the nations through His people
rationale: Ezekiel describes the holy name being profaned when nations see the Lord's people outside His land. Romans likewise says God's name is blasphemed among nations because of the addressed people's conduct, specifically their transgression of law.

relationship: repeated divine action for the sake of the profaned name
rationale: God spares Israel because of His holy name, profaned among nations. The earlier oracle similarly says God acted so His name would not be profaned at all before nations during Israel's departure from Egypt.

relationship: repeated distinction between Israel's conduct and God's concern for His name
rationale: Ezekiel says the coming action is for God's holy name rather than for Israel. The earlier wilderness account also attributes God's restraining action to protecting His name before the nations, despite the people's rebellion.

relationship: close parallel public sanctification before the nations
rationale: Both promises say God will be sanctified in the people before the nations' eyes. The earlier promise places this beside gathering them from dispersion, while the source emphasizes His profaned great name.

relationship: parallel gathering of dispersed Israel into its ancestral land
rationale: Both passages promise God's gathering of Israel from nations and bringing the people into their land. Deuteronomy describes that land as the fathers' inheritance and joins gathering with mercy and increase.

relationship: related sprinkling of water for purification
rationale: Ezekiel promises sprinkling clean water to cleanse the people from uncleannesses and idols. Numbers prescribes sprinkling purification water on persons and objects defiled by contact with death; the kinds of impurity and the water's preparation differ.

relationship: related combination of sprinkling, inward cleansing and pure water
rationale: Ezekiel's clean-water sprinkling removes uncleannesses and idols. Hebrews exhorts people to approach with hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and bodies washed with pure water, combining cleansing imagery in its exhortation about access to God.

relationship: close parallel replacement of the stone heart
rationale: Both promises give a new spirit and replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh. The earlier oracle says another heart, while the source says a new heart.

relationship: related contrast of stone and hearts of flesh with the Spirit
rationale: Ezekiel replaces a stone heart with a heart of flesh and gives a new spirit. Paul describes Christ's letter inscribed by the living God's Spirit on hearts of flesh rather than stone tablets; the writing metaphor differs from Ezekiel's replacement of a heart.

relationship: close parallel inner renewal enabling obedience
rationale: Both passages connect the gift of spirit within the people with walking in God's ordinances and doing His judgments or commands. Ezekiel 11 additionally states the reciprocal God-and-people relationship.

relationship: related Spirit-directed obedience to God's requirements
rationale: Ezekiel promises God's Spirit within the people so they keep His judgments. Romans describes God's action through His Son so the law's righteous requirement is fulfilled in those walking according to Spirit; it does not explicitly identify itself as this oracle's fulfillment.

relationship: shared restored covenant relationship
rationale: Both promises declare that the people will be God's people and He their God. Ezekiel locates them on the land given their fathers; Jeremiah joins the relationship with God's law written within their understanding and hearts.

relationship: parallel provision of grain after divine restoration
rationale: Ezekiel promises multiplied grain and relief from famine along with cleansing. Joel promises grain, wine and oil to satisfy the people and remove national reproach; the selected verse does not repeat Ezekiel's cleansing language.

relationship: parallel fruitful fields and trees ending food-related shame
rationale: Ezekiel multiplies tree fruit and field produce to remove the reproach of famine. Joel likewise promises fruitful trees, filled threshing floors and abundant eating, followed by the promise that God's people will not be put to shame.

relationship: close parallel remembrance of former evil with shame
rationale: Both promises describe remembering the ways by which Israel acted wickedly. The source expresses disgust at lawless deeds and abominations; the earlier oracle describes beating their faces because of their wickedness, without identical wording.

relationship: related denial that land possession rewards Israel's merit
rationale: Ezekiel says God is not acting because of Israel and calls the people to shame over their ways. Deuteronomy likewise denies that possession of the good land comes from Israel's righteous deeds or holy heart, calling the people stiff-necked.

relationship: parallel restoration and cleansing of national wrongdoing
rationale: Ezekiel joins cleansing from lawless deeds with inhabited cities and rebuilding. Jeremiah similarly joins restoration and rebuilding of Judah and Israel with cleansing of the injustices committed against God.

relationship: parallel cultivation replacing ruined land
rationale: Ezekiel says devastated land will again be worked. Amos describes restored Israelites rebuilding ruined cities and planting vineyards and gardens, giving concrete forms of renewed cultivation.

relationship: parallel transformation of devastated land into a garden
rationale: Ezekiel's devastated land becomes like a garden of delight. Isaiah likewise promises comfort to Zion's deserted places by making them like the Lord's paradise; neither comparison requires altering the source's garden wording.

relationship: parallel reversal from destruction to building and planting
rationale: Ezekiel identifies God as the One rebuilding razed places and planting devastated places. Jeremiah likewise contrasts His former tearing down and harming with His renewed watching to build and plant.

relationship: related explicit identification of human people with God's flock
rationale: Ezekiel promises to multiply human beings like sheep. The earlier shepherd oracle explicitly addresses the people as God's sheep and flock, supplying the same human-flock identification without the source's multiplication promise.

relationship: concrete festival-flock counterpart for the population comparison
rationale: Ezekiel compares cities full of people with Jerusalem's festival sheep. Chronicles describes many thousands of sheep, lambs and kids provided for Josiah's Passover; it illustrates large festival flocks without equating its numbers with Ezekiel's promised population.

relationship: repeated visionary setting involving the Lord's hand, a plain and spirit
rationale: The source places Ezekiel under the Lord's hand and brings him in spirit to a plain. The earlier commission likewise has the Lord's hand upon him, sends him to the plain and describes a spirit coming upon him; the visions there differ.

relationship: same-chapter explicit interpretation of the dry bones
rationale: The vision emphasizes the multitude and dryness of the bones. Its later interpretation identifies them as all Israel's house, whose saying about dry bones expresses lost hope and exhaustion.

relationship: question about renewed life alongside an assurance of the dead rising
rationale: God asks whether the bones will live, and Ezekiel leaves the answer to God's knowledge. Isaiah explicitly announces that the dead will rise and those in tombs awaken; Ezekiel's surrounding vision applies its bones to Israel's house.

relationship: related portrayal of the dead hearing a life-giving divine word
rationale: Ezekiel must tell dry bones to hear the Lord's word. Jesus says the dead will hear the Son of God's voice and live; Ezekiel's vision explains the bones as Israel's house rather than giving John's identical setting.

relationship: shared gift of the breath of life
rationale: God promises breath of life to the bones. Genesis describes God breathing the breath of life into the formed human so that he becomes a living soul; Ezekiel depicts restoration rather than the first human's formation.

relationship: shared description of bodily formation and divinely given life
rationale: Ezekiel names sinews, flesh and skin before the gift of Spirit and life. Job similarly recalls God clothing him in skin and flesh, joining bones and sinews, and granting life and care; the occasions differ.

relationship: same-chapter narrated commencement of the promised reconstruction
rationale: Ezekiel's obedient prophecy is followed by bones joining at their joints. This begins the earlier promised reconstitution of the bones with sinews, flesh and skin, while the complete gift of life remains later in the vision.

relationship: shared bodily materials with a significant difference about life
rationale: The vision shows sinews, flesh and skin on the bones but still no breath. Job recalls the same bodily materials together with God's gift of life and care, highlighting the distinction between bodily formation and living animation in Ezekiel's sequence.

relationship: related breathing of life into a formed body
rationale: Ezekiel calls the breath from the four winds to breathe into the dead so they live. Genesis describes God breathing life into the human formed from dust; Genesis does not supply the four winds or the multitude of bodies.

relationship: related breathing and reception of Spirit
rationale: The source commands breath to enter the dead and make them live. John describes Jesus breathing and telling the disciples to receive the Holy Spirit; this is a comparison of breathing and the divine gift of Spirit, not an identification of the disciples with Ezekiel's dead bodies.

relationship: same-chapter realization of the promised breath and life
rationale: After prophecy, breath enters the bodies, they live and stand. This realizes the earlier promise that God would put breath and Spirit into the bones so that they live.

relationship: related use of dried bones to express inward distress
rationale: Israel's saying that its bones are dry is explicitly joined with lost hope and exhaustion. Proverbs likewise says that a sorrowful person's bones dry up, using the bodily image for distress in an individual rather than the national vision.

relationship: parallel imagery of bringing life from tombs
rationale: Ezekiel promises to open the people's tombs and bring them into Israel's land. Isaiah announces that the dead will rise and those in tombs awaken; the selected Isaiah verse does not specify Ezekiel's return to Israel's land.

relationship: related image of people brought out of graves
rationale: Ezekiel links recognition of the Lord with His opening graves and bringing His people up. Jesus describes those in tombs hearing His voice and coming out to resurrection of life or judgment; Ezekiel's surrounding explanation concerns restoration of Israel's house.

relationship: related promise of life through God's indwelling Spirit
rationale: Ezekiel promises Spirit within the people, life and placement on their land. Romans promises that the One who raised Christ will give life to believers' mortal bodies through His indwelling Spirit; it does not include Ezekiel's land promise.

relationship: parallel use of inscribed tribal staffs as visible divine signs
rationale: Ezekiel writes Judah and Joseph-Ephraim on two staffs to depict joining. Numbers prescribes named staffs for ancestral houses, with Aaron's name on Levi's staff, for a sign of divine choosing; the signs and number of staffs differ.

relationship: contrasting actions with staffs concerning Judah and Israel
rationale: Ezekiel binds staffs into one in the sign of reunion. Zechariah throws away the second staff to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel; the source's joining contrasts with the target's throwing away without replacing its word possession.

relationship: parallel request for interpretation of a prophetic sign
rationale: Ezekiel anticipates the people's request to explain the staffs. In the earlier acted sign the people likewise ask what his conduct means, and he interprets the mourning sign; the visible actions themselves differ.

relationship: parallel reunion of Judah and Israel under common authority
rationale: The staff's interpretation joins Joseph-Ephraim and attached tribes to Judah as one staff in Judah's hand. Hosea likewise joins Judah's and Israel's sons gathering and appointing one authority; it does not use Ezekiel's staff imagery.

relationship: parallel public presentation of the tribal staffs
rationale: Ezekiel must hold the inscribed staffs before the people. Numbers describes Moses bringing the tribal staffs before all Israel, who look at them; the earlier context concerns the sprouted staff, whereas Ezekiel's sign concerns joining.

relationship: parallel gathering from nations into Israel's land
rationale: Both promises gather the dispersed people from nations and return them to their inherited land. Ezekiel expressly names all Israel's house and Israel's land.

relationship: close parallel reunion under a single ruler
rationale: Ezekiel promises one nation and ruler instead of two kingdoms. Hosea likewise promises Judah's and Israel's sons gathering together and appointing one authority.

relationship: repeated combination of cleansing from idols and covenant belonging
